image.subject: a slim man in his forties with a black mock turtleneck, jeans and sneakers, intense focused gaze, walking onto a dim stage in front of a large projection screen at an Apple product event in 1997

storyboard.claim: Jobs returned to Apple in 1997 after years away and had changed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jobs alone on a dark launch stage in front of a large screen, the 1997 Apple event.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the new answer to the question of why Campbell later backed Jobs.
storyboard.addedInformation: The year 1997 and the Apple return stage.

left.label: ROGUE
left.subject: a slim man in his forties with a black mock turtleneck, jeans and sneakers, intense focused gaze, jabbing a finger at a row of startled engineers in a crowded office

right.label: METICULOUS
right.subject: a slim man in his forties with a black mock turtleneck, jeans and sneakers, intense focused gaze, calmly reviewing a printed chart with two colleagues at a glass-walled conference table

storyboard.claim: Jobs changed from a rogue visionary into a meticulous manager.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two Jobs scenes side by side: the outburst and the calm chart review.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the return to Apple by showing the before and after.
storyboard.addedInformation: The contrast between the old outbursts and the new discipline.

image.subject: a glass-walled Silicon Valley office with a whiteboard covered in a neat supply-chain flow diagram and stacks of printed operations reports on a long conference table, no people

storyboard.claim: Jobs built a disciplined operational system.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A whiteboard with a tidy supply-chain diagram in an office with no people.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Makes the shift from temper to method concrete.
storyboard.addedInformation: The operational machinery he built.

storyboard.claim: Jobs learned to run finance, logistics and supply chains.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A three-line list of the operational skills he learned.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Lists the specifics behind the disciplined manager.
storyboard.addedInformation: The three skill areas he took on.

image.subject: a slim man in his forties with a black mock turtleneck, jeans and sneakers, intense focused gaze, leaning on the back of a chair beside three engineers gathered in a team huddle around a laptop in an office

storyboard.claim: Jobs surrounded himself with operators and became a team builder, still demanding.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jobs in a team huddle with three engineers around a laptop.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the operations skills to the people around him.
storyboard.addedInformation: He still demanded a lot but now worked as part of a team.

image.subject: a slim man in his forties with a black mock turtleneck, jeans and sneakers, intense focused gaze, standing at a whiteboard drawing a connected system of boxes and arrows while two engineers take notes

storyboard.claim: Jobs ran a coordinated system instead of throwing tantrums.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jobs at a whiteboard drawing linked boxes and arrows, engineers taking notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reframes the earlier tantrum image as a managed system.
storyboard.addedInformation: The system is drawn out as a process of connected parts.

image.subject: a woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, sitting across a desk from a colleague, both leaning over one shared laptop and laughing together

storyboard.claim: Trust and cohesion of the team matter more than any one talent.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager and a colleague sharing a laptop across a desk, relaxed and working together.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the principle the Jobs example just illustrated.
storyboard.addedInformation: Team cohesion is valued above individual talent.

storyboard.claim: A team that is destroyed takes the product down with it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only quotation of the warning.
storyboard.onScreenText: If they destroy the team, they destroy the product eventually.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the principle into a warning.
storyboard.addedInformation: The team is the foundation of the product.

image.subject: an empty chair pushed back from a glass conference table in an office, a leather laptop bag beside it and the doorway open to a hallway

storyboard.claim: Toxic geniuses are cut loose to protect the team.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An empty chair pushed back from a conference table with the door open.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the warning to the choice of who stays.
storyboard.addedInformation: Removing the toxic person is an act of protection.

image.subject: an open desk calendar with one-on-one meetings blocked out in neat rows, a pen resting across the page

storyboard.claim: A manager must decide where to spend scarce management time.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A desk calendar with one-on-one slots blocked out.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Asks who to invest time in after cutting the toxic genius.
storyboard.addedInformation: Management time is scarce and has to be spent deliberately.

image.subject: Bill Campbell: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, leaning forward across a desk to interview a young candidate in a glass-walled office

storyboard.claim: Campbell chooses who to invest in by selecting the people who will build the team with him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell leaning across a desk toward a young candidate.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the question of time to the question of who to pick.
storyboard.addedInformation: Campbell is shown as the one doing the selecting.

image.subject: a tense tech company boardroom with a wooden table and a projector screen showing a falling stock line, directors sitting in silence around the table

storyboard.claim: The company missed its targets in a rough quarter and the stock is falling.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A silent boardroom with a falling stock chart on the projector screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets the scene for the selection example.
storyboard.addedInformation: The crisis that the board must respond to.

image.subject: Bill Campbell: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, sitting at the head of a boardroom table with a printed budget in front of him

storyboard.claim: Campbell as CEO wants to cut costs and enforce discipline.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell seated at the head of the boardroom table with a budget in front of him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces Campbell in the CEO chair during the crisis.
storyboard.addedInformation: His instinct is lean cost discipline.

left.label: CEO
left.subject: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, holding a spreadsheet and tapping its numbers

right.label: BOARD
right.subject: a row of board directors in dark suits on the far side of a wooden boardroom table, arms folded, shaking their heads

storyboard.claim: The whole board disagrees with Campbell's financial strategy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell with his spreadsheet facing a row of directors with folded arms.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the standoff that the cost plan creates.
storyboard.addedInformation: The board wants to spend, not cut.

image.subject: a glossy marketing poster propped on an easel in a bright office, with a few directors in suits studying it and nodding

storyboard.claim: The board wants to spend heavily on marketing and future development.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A glossy marketing poster on an easel with directors studying it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States what the board wants instead of Campbell's cuts.
storyboard.addedInformation: Spending on future development despite the short-term hit.

image.subject: a silver-haired man in a dark suit leaning forward at a boardroom table, one hand raised to speak while the other directors turn to listen

storyboard.claim: The venture capitalist John Doerr, a board member, speaks up.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A silver-haired man in a dark suit raising a hand at the boardroom table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the board member who breaks the standoff.
storyboard.addedInformation: The speaker is a venture capitalist on the board.

storyboard.claim: The board member says to back the coach.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only quotation of the line.
storyboard.onScreenText: I think we should back the coach.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The pivotal line after the standoff.
storyboard.addedInformation: The board chooses trust in Campbell over agreement on numbers.

image.subject: a printed spreadsheet lying untouched on a boardroom table beside two clasped hands

storyboard.claim: Trust is not about agreeing on the spreadsheet.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An untouched spreadsheet next to clasped hands on a table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains what the back the coach line means.
storyboard.addedInformation: Trust sits apart from the numbers.

image.subject: Bill Campbell: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, shaking hands across a boardroom table with a smiling board director

storyboard.claim: The board thought the numbers were wrong but trusted Campbell as a person.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell and a director shaking hands across the boardroom table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the reason the board backed a plan they doubted.
storyboard.addedInformation: Trust in the person, not the spreadsheet.

image.subject: a woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, sitting across a desk from a colleague, looking up from her notes with a questioning expression

storyboard.claim: Trust is earned by integrity to pivot and grit to execute, and managers should ask whether they can back their people.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager pausing over her notes at her desk and looking up, questioning.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the board example into a question for the viewer's own team.
storyboard.addedInformation: Two qualities that make someone worth backing.

storyboard.claim: Ask whether you back people even when their metrics look terrifying.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question for the manager.
storyboard.onScreenText: Can you back people when their metrics look terrifying?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the manager question into the key test.
storyboard.addedInformation: The test is backing people whose strategy differs from yours.

image.subject: Bill Campbell: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, listening intently across a desk while a young engineer speaks, head slightly tilted

storyboard.claim: The raw material to look for is humility, the ability to be coached.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell listening attentively to a young engineer across a desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the key indicator of someone worth backing.
storyboard.addedInformation: Humility is shown as active listening.

image.subject: two men in a small Silicon Valley office: Jonathan Rosenberg, a man in his fifties with short dark hair and a light blazer, engaged and conversational, seated across a desk from Bill Campbell, a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket

storyboard.claim: Jonathan Rosenberg's final interview before joining Google shows how strictly Campbell screened.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Rosenberg and Campbell facing each other across a desk in a small office.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the story of the screening interview.
storyboard.addedInformation: The interview takes place before Rosenberg joined Google.

image.subject: Jonathan Rosenberg: a man in his fifties with short dark hair and a light blazer, engaged and conversational, leaning back in an office chair with a relaxed, sure-of-himself smile

storyboard.claim: Rosenberg is confident he has the job locked.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Rosenberg leaning back in his chair with a sure smile.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up Rosenberg's overconfidence before the interview turns.
storyboard.addedInformation: He believes the job is basically secured.

image.subject: Bill Campbell: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, staring fixedly across a desk at a visitor without speaking, eyebrows raised

storyboard.claim: Campbell skips skills and stares, asking one simple question.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell staring silently across a desk with raised eyebrows.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shifts from Rosenberg's confidence to Campbell's silent pressure.
storyboard.addedInformation: No questions about technical skills or strategy.

storyboard.claim: Campbell asks whether the candidate is coachable.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question on screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers the one simple question.
storyboard.addedInformation: Coachability is the single test.

image.subject: Jonathan Rosenberg: a man in his fifties with short dark hair and a light blazer, engaged and conversational, leaning back with arms crossed and a smug smile, answering across a desk

storyboard.claim: Rosenberg arrogantly answers that it depends.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Rosenberg leaning back with arms crossed and a smug smile.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the wrong answer to the coachability question.
storyboard.addedInformation: The answer shows executive ego.

storyboard.claim: It is the worst possible answer to give Campbell.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only punchline.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Judges the answer just given.
storyboard.addedInformation: Campbell rejects conditional commitment.

image.subject: Bill Campbell: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, leaning forward across a desk toward Jonathan Rosenberg, a man in his fifties with short dark hair and a light blazer, who sits upright and looks uneasy

storyboard.claim: Campbell forces Rosenberg to define what a coach is.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell leaning in over the desk while Rosenberg sits upright, uneasy.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Campbell does not let the arrogant answer slide.
storyboard.addedInformation: Rosenberg is pressed to explain the idea of coaching.

image.subject: a football resting on a glass conference table beside an open notebook, with a sport jacket draped over a chair

storyboard.claim: Rosenberg pulls out a quote from the football coach Tom Landry.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A football and open notebook on a conference table with a jacket on a chair.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the stumble that leads to the quote.
storyboard.addedInformation: The football coach who gave the quote.

storyboard.claim: A coach makes you see what you do not want to see so you can be who you want to be.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only quotation of the Landry line.
storyboard.onScreenText: You see what you don't want to see so you can be who you want to be.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The quote Rosenberg manages to produce.
storyboard.addedInformation: The Landry line defines the coach's role.

image.subject: Bill Campbell: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, standing in an office doorway with a hand on the frame, listening warmly to a younger colleague mid-sentence

storyboard.claim: Campbell invests his time and political capital only in people with humility.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell in a doorway listening warmly to a younger colleague.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Generalises the Rosenberg lesson.
storyboard.addedInformation: Political capital is spent only on the humble.

image.subject: a printed resume with a red line through its top half lying on a glass conference table

storyboard.claim: Without coachability, a strong resume gets you nothing with Campbell.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A resume crossed out in red on a glass table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concludes the screening lesson.
storyboard.addedInformation: A resume cannot make up for missing humility.

storyboard.claim: In corporate culture coachability is often a code word for obedience.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question on screen.
storyboard.onScreenText: Is coachability just a code word for obedience?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The host challenges the definition of coachability.
storyboard.addedInformation: The reading of coachability as obedience is raised.

image.subject: a row of identical office workers in gray suits nodding in unison at a manager standing at the front of a conference room

storyboard.claim: Obedience means doing what you are told and never arguing with the boss.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A row of gray-suited workers nodding in unison at a manager at the front.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the obedience reading the hosts are challenging.
storyboard.addedInformation: Dissent is absent in this picture.

left.label: DISSENT
left.subject: a heated meeting at a glass conference table, several people talking at once and gesturing toward a whiteboard

right.label: OBEDIENCE
right.subject: a silent row of employees in gray suits nodding at a man at the head of the table

storyboard.claim: Campbell wanted debate and broke ties, so he did not want obedience.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A heated debate on the left and a silent row of nodding staff on the right.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Argues against the obedience reading using the tie-breaking point.
storyboard.addedInformation: Campbell valued dissent before breaking a tie.

image.subject: three founders standing close together in a bright Silicon Valley office: a slim man in his forties with a black mock turtleneck, jeans and sneakers, intense focused gaze in the centre; a young man in his late twenties with tousled brown hair and a casual sweater, thoughtful expression on the left; a young man in his late twenties with curly dark hair and a casual open shirt, animated expression on the right

storyboard.claim: Campbell championed Steve Jobs, Larry Page and Sergey Brin.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Three founders standing together: Jobs in the centre, Page on the left, Brin on the right.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the evidence the hosts promised.
storyboard.addedInformation: The three founders Campbell backed.

storyboard.claim: None of these founders were obedient; they were independent and pushed back.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A three-line list of what the founders were like.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Supports the argument with the founders described.
storyboard.addedInformation: They were difficult founders who constantly challenged others.

storyboard.claim: Coachability in Campbell's framework is not obedience but the absence of BS.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only quotation of the definition.
storyboard.onScreenText: Coachability isn't obedience. It is the absence of BS.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the working definition after the evidence.
storyboard.addedInformation: The reframed meaning of coachability.

storyboard.claim: The absence of BS means honesty, including looking at a failure and admitting it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question on screen.
storyboard.onScreenText: What does the absence of BS look like?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The host asks for the practical meaning of the definition.
storyboard.addedInformation: Honesty is the capacity to face a major failure.
